items.headline: Wiz's GhostApproval turns a repo symlink into an SSH-key write across six AI coding agents
items.diff_narrative: New today: Wiz Research's GhostApproval, disclosed July 8 and absent from yesterday's report, turns the decades-old symbolic link into a repository-borne attack on AI coding assistants. A malicious repo ships a file with a benign name such as project_settings.json that is actually a symlink to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys; when a developer asks the agent to set up the workspace and approves what looks like a harmless config edit, the write lands on the SSH file instead, planting an attacker's key for passwordless remote access. The core failure is a consent bypass — the approval dialog shows only the innocuous filename, never the sensitive path it resolves to. Wiz reported it to six vendors: Amazon Q Developer (CVE-2026-12958), Anthropic's Claude Code, Augment, Cursor (CVE-2026-50549), Google Antigravity, and Windsurf; Amazon, Cursor, and Google shipped fixes, Augment and Windsurf were unpatched at disclosure, and Anthropic disputed that Claude Code's behavior is a bug at all, arguing a developer who trusts a directory owns the approval. Where yesterday's AI Now Institute proof-of-concept had an agent execute a README-hidden payload during an audit and argued no patch was possible by design, today's flaw redirects the agent's file write onto a sensitive path and drew a conventional multi-vendor CVE response — with the industry openly split on whether silently following a symlink is the tool's vulnerability or the user's mistake.

items.headline: TUM's ThorArena benchmark exposes how humanoid controllers fail under real contact forces
items.diff_narrative: New today: the Technical University of Munich published ThorArena on arXiv, opening a robotics front absent from yesterday's report. The benchmark stress-tests humanoid whole-body control under deliberate, load-bearing contact — active force exchange rather than collision avoidance. The team captured synchronized whole-body motion and hand forces from human operators wearing VR headsets, motion trackers, and 3D-printed force-sensing tools across six contact-rich chores — lifting and lowering a water container, pushing and pulling a chair, and co-carrying an object with a partner — then replayed those forces in simulation against representative control policies. Its Force-Aware Tracking Score jointly grades tracking accuracy, robustness across force levels, control effort, and whether the robot stays upright to the end of the episode. The headline result: force-informed evaluation exposes large performance gaps that stay invisible under conventional no-force testing, and the authors' own Thor2 policy was the only entry to hold near-perfect balance across all six tasks. It lands as Figure, Agility, and Boston Dynamics push humanoids from pilots into factories and warehouses, where a person will inevitably lean on, push, or hand something to the robot — precisely the regime today's controllers handle worst.

items.headline: Micron raises its US investment to $250 billion and pours first concrete at its New York megafab
items.diff_narrative: New today: Micron said on July 9 it is raising its planned US investment to more than $250 billion through 2035 — a $50 billion increase over the $200 billion plan set in mid-2025 — and framed the bump squarely as a response to AI-era memory demand. The announcement coincided with the first concrete pour at its Clay, New York site, more than a quarter ahead of schedule, marking the shift from site preparation to vertical construction on what Micron says will become the largest semiconductor manufacturing site in US history; the company reiterated a goal of producing 40% of its DRAM on US soil. It extends the memory-capacity thread that yesterday's SK Hynix Nasdaq listing opened, from a different angle: yesterday was a $26.5 billion financing event that converted the HBM supply story into tradeable capital, while today is a manufacturing-capacity commitment poured into concrete. As the source frames it, HBM stacks and advanced DRAM are sold out well into the future, and Micron's raise lands days after SK Hynix earmarked its listing proceeds for EUV-equipped capacity — two of the three big memory makers committing fresh capital to the same AI-accelerator bottleneck in the same week.

items.headline: AI events calendar: Ray Summit locks August 24-26 dates as AMD Advancing AI July 22-23 stays the nearest stop
items.diff_narrative: Updated from yesterday's calendar: the standout change is Anyscale's Ray Summit, which firms from an undated 'late-August program' to hard dates — August 24-26 at the San Francisco Marriott Marquis, a training day plus two days on scaling LLM and reinforcement-learning workloads. AMD Advancing AI stays the nearest stop at Moscone West on July 22-23, now with sharper detail: Lisa Su is expected to detail the Instinct MI450 accelerator and Zen 6 EPYC 'Venice' CPUs, where yesterday's note read only 'MI4xx-series positioning against Blackwell.' Black Hat USA gains firm dates (August 1-6) alongside DEF CON 34's AI Village, and the AI Risk Summit (August 11-12), Ai4 (August 4-6), Hot Chips with its July 31 early rate, AI Infra Summit, OWASP Global AppSec, ACM AI Leadership Summit, The AI Conference, GitHub Universe, AWS re:Invent, and NeurIPS all carry over. The near-term actions drop yesterday's Sol Ultra framing note and now simply point at registering for AMD before July 22, locking the July 31 Hot Chips rate, and booking Black Hat plus the AI Risk Summit for the early-August security block.
